# Descriptive Statistics and Graphs {.unnumbered}

Description answers what was observed: how many participants were analysed, how variables were distributed, which values were missing, and how groups differed in their observed characteristics. A descriptive table should therefore identify the denominator and measurement unit, not merely display numbers.

The next two chapters address numerical summaries and graphical presentation. Use both. A mean and standard deviation can conceal skewness, multiple peaks, or an influential observation. A graph can reveal those features but may not communicate the exact count or estimate needed for reporting. The NIST handbook describes these complementary numerical and graphical approaches to exploratory analysis. [@NISTHist; @NISTScale]

Describe the data before comparing groups. This order helps identify coding problems and clarifies which statistical quantity would answer the question. A choice between a mean and a median should reflect the objective and distribution, rather than a rule that every variable must be reduced to the same summary.

By the end of this part, the reader should be able to construct a descriptive table, select a suitable graph, and explain the important features of an observed distribution.
